title: Invest In Junior Engineers
gist: An EDA industry veteran argues that replacing junior engineers with AI agents is short-term thinking that breaks the pipeline producing senior engineers and destroys the organization's main source of new-architecture exploration. He cites CS graduate unemployment now exceeding the average — a historical inversion — and uses the RTL/logic-synthesis transition, where juniors rather than incumbents drove adoption, as evidence that the displaced cohort is precisely the one that adopts disruptive tooling.

themes.theme: Labor market inversion for engineering entrants

insights.claim: Unemployment among new computer science graduates is now higher than the overall average, reversing a relationship that had always run the other way, and enrollment is expected to fall as a result.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: A structural break in the entry-level tech labor market is the earliest observable evidence that AI is substituting rather than augmenting; it precedes any productivity data in company filings.
insights.quote: The unemployment rate for them is now higher than the average, something that has always been the reverse in the past.
insights.locator: There are numerous reports about new graduates

insights.claim: Falling CS enrollment is attributed partly to AI being increasingly viewed negatively among younger people, meaning the pipeline contraction is driven by sentiment as well as by job availability.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Sentiment-driven enrollment decline takes 4+ years to reverse, so any future engineering shortage is already largely locked in.
insights.quote: Enrollment will likely drop, especially since AI is increasingly being seen in a negative light amongst the younger population.
insights.locator: There are numerous reports about new graduates

insights.claim: AI displacement of engineers is furthest along in general software development specifically because abundant freely available code exists to train on, and whether that capability extends to embedded software remains uncertain.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Training-data availability, not task difficulty, predicts where AI displaces labor first — a usable screen for which engineering disciplines are exposed next.
insights.quote: especially in the software development world where there are lots of freely available examples on which AI can be trained. Whether that can expand into embedded software is still somewhat uncertain.
insights.locator: How many junior engineers can be replaced by AI

insights.claim: In semiconductors the displacement is described as moving more slowly than in software but showing signs of accelerating, placing the chip industry roughly one cycle behind the software labor shock.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: A lagged but accelerating adoption curve in chip design means EDA headcount effects are still ahead, not behind, for design-services and IP firms.
insights.quote: In the semiconductor space things are moving a little slower, but there are signs that it is accelerating.
insights.locator: In the semiconductor space things are moving

themes.theme: Verification as the first agentic AI beachhead

insights.claim: Agentic AI is reported as being used in chip verification with a fair level of success, making verification the identified first production beachhead for autonomous agents in semiconductor design flows.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Verification is the largest labor pool in chip design; agent success there is where EDA vendors first convert AI into seat-price or consumption revenue.
insights.quote: A common message is that agentic AI is being used in the verification space and having a fair level of success.
insights.locator: In the semiconductor space things are moving

insights.claim: Companies simultaneously insist verification demand can never be satisfied — you can never do enough of it or do it quickly enough — so agent-driven productivity is expected to be absorbed by rising complexity rather than converted into headcount cuts at the discipline level.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Jevons-style absorption in verification means AI adoption expands tool consumption rather than shrinking the market — bullish for verification tool vendors.
insights.quote: you can never do enough verification, and you can never do it quickly enough
insights.locator: At the same time, most companies are saying

insights.claim: The predicted demise of verification has repeatedly failed to materialize while demand and complexity kept growing, which the author uses as the base rate against which to judge current AI-replaces-verification claims.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: A documented history of false obsolescence calls is a reason to discount current claims that AI collapses verification spend.
insights.quote: The demise of verification has been portended many times in the past, and yet the demands have continued to grow, and the problem becomes increasingly complex.
insights.locator: At the same time, most companies are saying

insights.claim: The author flags an unresolved contradiction: even if verification as a discipline survives and grows, the junior verification engineers within it are already being displaced, so aggregate discipline health masks cohort-level destruction.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Headcount totals will hide the composition shift; the seniority mix inside engineering orgs is the metric that actually signals AI penetration.
insights.quote: But what about those junior verification engineers who have been displaced?
insights.locator: The demise of verification has been portended

themes.theme: The AI value proposition to juniors was misaimed

insights.claim: The original chatbot pitch — that juniors would no longer need to master complex EDA tools or language syntax — targeted skills that budding engineers already acquire quickly, so the claimed benefit addressed a low-value bottleneck.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: AI tooling that automates fast-to-learn skills captures little real value; the durable products will target judgment-adjacent work instead.
insights.quote: But none of this really takes long for a budding engineer. They can pick most of this up fairly quickly, but okay, AI could help them do that quicker. Still, that isn’t what makes them a senior engineer.
insights.locator: The first round of AI introductions, the chatbots

insights.claim: Seniority is defined as experience, judgment, and the ability to do things AI cannot yet capture — none of which are acquired by using AI to bypass the tool-and-syntax learning stage.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: If judgment is built through the tasks AI now performs, automating them severs the training path — a delayed but compounding organizational cost.
insights.quote: That requires experience, judgment, and being able to do the things that cannot be captured by AI yet.
insights.locator: The first round of AI introductions, the chatbots

insights.claim: The core succession problem is posed directly: if junior engineers have no value, there is no mechanism by which they become the senior engineers needed to replace the retiring cohort, so a development path for every engineering level must be constructed deliberately.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Firms cutting entry-level engineering are borrowing against a senior-talent shortage that arrives on a retirement schedule, not a business-cycle one.
insights.quote: if junior engineers have no value, how do they become senior engineers? Eventually, they will be needed to replace the current senior engineers as they retire.
insights.locator: Two things are cause for concern

themes.theme: Historical precedent: juniors drive disruptive adoption

insights.claim: When RTL and logic synthesis first appeared, the incumbent senior logic designers disliked and resisted the technology because they could beat it and it threatened to displace them, while junior engineers with nothing to lose adopted it and proved it out.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: The cohort most incentivized to adopt disruptive tooling is the one being cut; eliminating juniors removes the organization's adoption mechanism for the next disruption.
insights.quote: It was junior engineers, who had nothing to lose, who adopted synthesis and showed that while the senior engineers could still beat them on PPA, they could do it in a fraction of the time.

insights.claim: The synthesis transition succeeded because the productivity gain exceeded the power/performance/area quality sacrificed — a general rule for judging whether an automation technology wins despite producing inferior point results.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Apply the same test to AI-generated RTL: adoption turns on the productivity-versus-quality ratio, not on whether AI output beats an expert.
insights.quote: The productivity boost was significantly greater than the PPA they were giving up.

insights.claim: Exploring new device technologies is argued to be better suited to junior engineers than to architects, because seniors become set in their ways and their time is more valuably spent shipping production systems — an inversion of the usual assumption that architecture exploration is a senior role.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Cheap exploratory capacity is what juniors uniquely provide; cutting them concentrates all technology-evaluation risk in people who have no time for it.
insights.quote: Normally, we think that is the role of the senior engineer or architect, but they can become stuck in their ways, and perhaps they are not the best equipped when it comes to researching new devices or new possibilities.
insights.locator: There is often an overlooked opportunity

insights.claim: The author's own formative assignment — determining whether early PALs could shrink a two-board avionics system onto one board — explicitly did not require a production-worthy design, only a demonstration of a new architecture, and it failed on the first attempt without that being a problem.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Tolerating failed exploratory projects is the organizational capability at risk; AI-efficiency metrics implicitly penalize exactly this kind of work.
insights.quote: This was not about whether I could create the perfect design, or even one that would be worthy of a production system. It was to see if I could demonstrate a new architecture.
insights.locator: There is often an overlooked opportunity

themes.theme: Organizational prescription and the agent-management trap

insights.claim: If senior engineers are occupied managing ten or more AI agents, they lose the time to do the things AI cannot do — meaning the agent-supervision model consumes precisely the scarce human capacity it was meant to leverage.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Agent-per-engineer ratios are being sold as productivity but function as a hidden tax on senior judgment; watch for it showing up as slower architectural innovation.
insights.quote: If senior engineers are busy managing 10 or more agents, they do not have the time to do other things. They do not have a lot of time to do the things that AI cannot do.
insights.locator: It may be enticing to reduce the number of junior engineers

insights.claim: The prevailing 'adopt AI or be left behind' imperative is accepted but held to be insufficient on its own; companies must simultaneously reimagine every engineering role and invest in employees to remain competitive once AI handles all the easy work.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Competitive advantage post-automation accrues to firms that restructured roles, not to those that merely deployed tools — a differentiator not visible in AI spend disclosures.
insights.quote: The general thinking today is, ‘Adopt AI or be left behind.’

insights.claim: The author proposes a new organizational role — a 'people architect' responsible for transforming the development process and defining how humans and AI fit into it — as the structural answer to the junior-engineer problem.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: A named role for human-AI process design is an early marker of how firms will operationalize AI; its emergence in job postings would confirm the thesis.
insights.quote: Perhaps companies need to have a people architect, someone who can transform the development process and how humans and AI fit into it.

insights.claim: Training must target what a senior engineer will be expected to do in five to ten years — which the author states is certainly not what seniors do today — making current job descriptions a poor basis for workforce planning.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Skills planning anchored on present-day role definitions is structurally wrong; firms training to today's job spec are misallocating development budget.
insights.quote: How do you train junior engineers to be what a senior engineer will be expected to do in five or ten years, which is certainly not what they are doing today?
insights.locator: It may be enticing to reduce the number of junior engineers
